title: The Last Samurai
full_review:
An embittered Civil War veteran finds himself fighting to reclaim his soul and that of a nation in director Edward Zwick's epic costume drama "The Last Samurai" (Warner Bros.).

Lavishly shot with painstaking attention to historical detail, the East-meets-West spectacle is, at its center, an intimate tale of one man's search for redemption. Unfortunately, despite lofty platitudes about honor, the film's gilded portrayal of the warriors' militaristic lifestyle and hail-of-bullets climax results in an at times overly romantic view of war.

Set in 1876, the film stars Tom Cruise as Capt. Nathan Algren, a burned-out ex-cavalryman whose tours of duty in the Union army and as a soldier under General Custer during the brutal Indian campaigns have left him disillusioned and scarred with self-loathing. While working as a drunken shill for the Winchester rifle company, he is hired by the young emperor of Japan (Shichinosuke Nakamura) to mold the country's first conscript army into a modern mechanized militia. Arriving in the land of the Rising Sun, Algren finds that the Imperial "army" is in fact a motley battalion of gun-shy peasants mentally ill-equipped for combat.

As he whips them into shape, Algren finds himself entangled in an internecine power struggle between two men vying for the weak-willed emperor's ear. On the one side is Minister Omura (Masato Harada), a capitalist bureaucrat who, wooed by American trade interests, is trying to Westernize the country and lift Japan's 200-year-old isolationist policy. Set against him is Katsumoto (Ken Watanabe), a samurai general who, along with his band of renegade warriors, is intent on preserving the "old ways and traditions." Omura realizes that Katsumoto's fealty to the emperor threatens his plans of modernization, but the samurai will not go down without a fight.

Desperate to suppress the samurai's last-ditch rebellion in the provinces, Omura -- against Algren's counsel -- thrusts the emperor's forces into combat prematurely. Despite the advantage of modern firearms, the green recruits prove no match for the outnumbered but battle-tested samurai. During the fray, Algren is captured and carried off to Katsumoto's mountain retreat. Katsumoto, a ferocious but high-minded warrior-poet, spares Algren's life, much more interested in understanding his "enemy" than fighting him.

Captor and captive quickly develop a spiritual affinity for each other -- both men are tired of the battlefield yet tethered to it. Algren begins to embrace their chivalrous code of "bushido" -- or "way of the warrior." Life in the hamlet proves an effective balm for his guilt-ridden soul. But Algren's Zen tranquility is shattered when he learns that in his absence the imperial army has been forged into a formidable fighting machine, buttressed by Western-style artillery, including Gatling guns and howitzers. Algren decides to make his last stand with the obsolescing samurai -- even if it is a losing cause.

Cruise, who will probably commit seppuku (ritual disembowelment) if he leaves the Oscars empty-handed again, delivers a strong performance as the dissolute ex-patriot, reining in his typical hammy Hollywood style in favor of a more beveled emotional nuance, communicating much through silence.

Visually, "The Last Samurai" echoes the pageantry of legendary Japanese filmmaker Akira Kurosawa's sword sagas. John Toll's eloquent cinematography captures the natural beauty of the Japanese landscape -- imbuing the idyllic village with both a weathered realism and the impressionistic simplicity of a haiku. And while the stunning battle sequences are extremely bloody, the choreography of carnage is executed with balletic precision.

Eschewing computer-generated troops, Zwick wages war the old-fashioned way, with hundreds of flesh-and-blood extras. The story, however, would have been better served if Cruise had used his samurai sword to slice some of the narrative fat off the film's 2:26 running time.

While the film's violence is essential to the telling of the tale, its espousal of such ideals as honor and valor is flawed by an exalted view of war which paints death in battle as gloriously heroic rather than tragic (a departure from Zwick's less blood-lusty Civil War film "Glory"). And while proper respect should be shown to foreign customs and value systems, the notion of death before dishonor taken to such an extreme as to justify suicide rather than "losing face" is totally inconsistent with Christianity's inviolable prohibition against the taking of one's own life. The unquestioning devotion to martial precepts and anti-Western sentiment idealized in the film led to the horrors of World War II and fueled kamikaze dive bombers.

And though "Samurai" raises important cultural questions about the cost of modernity and the value of tradition, it subscribes to the fashionable trend of painting people of Western culture as inherently corrupt and morally inferior to their Eastern counterparts. While the movie portrays the Japanese as honorable (except for the sell-out Omura), it depicts white men (excluding the Nipponized Algren) at best as sniveling opportunists and at worst as genocidal goons like Algren's former commanding officer (Tony Goldwyn).

At one point Algren is asked, "What is it about your people that you hate so much?" Perhaps the same could be asked of Mr. Zwick.

Due to strong battlefield violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
